title: Preference for Curvilinear Contour in Interior Architectural Spaces: Evidence From Experts and Nonexperts
research_question: To test the hypothesis that expertise moderates one's sensitivity to curvilinear contour within architectural spaces, specifically examining its effect on aesthetic judgments (beauty) and approach-avoidance decisions (willingness to enter/exit).

participants.description: 71 self-identified architects and designers (experts; 45 female, 21 male, 5 unspecified; 80% aged 21-60) and 71 undergraduate/graduate students (nonexperts; 45 female, 26 male; 87% aged 21-60) with no architecture/design expertise.
participants.recruitment: Experts collected booklets at a seminar. Nonexperts were approached in institution halls and invited to take part.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 8 color images of interior architectural spaces, 4 with curvilinear contours and 4 with rectilinear contours. Selected from a larger pool used in Vartanian et al. (2013).

nonexpert participants were more likely to rate the images as beautiful (.60, 95% CI [.54, .66]) than expert participants (.50, 95% CI [.44, .56]).

findings.mechanism: as designers of spaces, contour is a more salient variable to architects and designers than it is to nonexpert participants.

findings.quote: Task order had no effect on participants' responses to the enter task (b = .004, z = 0.024, p = .981).

mechanisms: For experts' greater sensitivity to contour in beauty judgments: contour is a more salient variable for architects/designers; or negative associations toward rectilinear contours honed through professional practice/training.

For nonexperts' greater sensitivity to contour in approach-avoidance decisions: functionality or usability of a space becomes the relevant frame for choice; experts may view images dispassionately, less subject to implicit behavioral biases.
Greater viewing time might trigger top-down processes that alter initial rapid response to contour, and this alteration might vary by task (beauty vs. approach-avoidance).
moderators: Task order (beauty judgment first vs. willingness to enter first)
implementation_implications: Contour is an important and potentially adaptive visual feature in architecture and design.
Expertise impacts the aesthetic and motivational relevance of contour.
limitations: Relatively small number of stimuli (8 images).
Use of dichotomous scales for beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions (more fine-grained responses could be collected with scales offering more than two options).
Context within which data were collected varied between experts and nonexperts (seminar vs. university halls), suggesting future studies should aim for identical conditions.
